title: The last tender is not the all-aboard time.
subtitle: It is earlier, it is a separate number, and it is where port days quietly go wrong.

text: A tender port has two deadlines and you only read one.
sub: All-aboard is the moment the gangway closes. The last tender is the moment the last boat leaves the shore — and a full boat takes twenty minutes to load and cross.

title: Four ways a tender day turns

items.head: Moderate swell suspends the service
items.body: Wind, swell or poor visibility is enough. The ship sits in plain sight of a port you cannot reach.

items.head: The queue is the excursion
items.body: Ship's tours board first. Independents wait, and on a full ship that wait can run past an hour.

items.head: One boat, not four
items.body: Late in the day the service thins out. The last tender is genuinely the last one.

items.head: The swell builds while you're ashore
items.body: Tendering can be cut short. Being back early is not caution here, it is the plan.

right.label: Alongside
items: You walk off when you like

text: Smaller ships berth where large ones must anchor.
sub: That is not a marketing line — it is why the same itinerary on a smaller vessel loses fewer ports. When I compare two sailings, I count how many calls are tendered.

quote: Ask which calls are tendered before you ask about the suite. One of those answers changes your week.

title: Save this before your next port-heavy itinerary
body: Or send me the sailing and I'll mark which calls are tendered, which dock, and which two days have no margin worth spending.
